full_judgment:
Sultan Hossain Khan J.- This rule has been referred to this Bench by the learned Chief Justice for a decision since contrary views with regard to the question whether an application for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 (hereinafter referred to as the Act) would fail in absence of a finding by the trial Court as to the eligibility of a pre-emptor u/s 90 of the Act to pre-empt a transfer have been expressed by some Single Benches of this Court. 

 2. The petitioners as pre-emptors filed an application u/s 96 of the Act to pre-empt the transfer. The said application was contested by the pre-emptee-opposite parties on the sole ground that the application was barred by limitation. The learned Munsif on hearing the petition allowed it. The learned Subordinate Judge, on appeal though upheld the findings of the learned Munsif on limitation, allowed the appeal and dismissed the pre-emption case on the ground, that the application was bad for defect of parties and that the learned Munsif failed to record any finding on the point as to whether the pre-emption petitioners are persons entitled to pre-empt the transfer under section 90 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Upon these two grounds the appeal was allowed and the application for pre-emption was dismissed. This rule under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge. 

 3. Mr. Abdur Rahim, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners has submitted that the written objection filed before the learned Munsif does not contain any specific allegation that any co-sharer or contiguous tenant had not been impleaded or joined in the application. He has next submitted that although written objection contains a general allegation that the application for pre-emption is bad for defect of parties there is no specific allegation of non-joinder of a necessary party. Mr. Abdur Rahim has contended that the objection as to omission of a necessary party must be taken at the earliest opportunity and if no such objection is taken, it may be deemed that the defect had been waived. This controversy as to non-joinder of co-sharer or a contiguous tenant has been set at rest by a decision of the Appellate Division of this Court in the case of Akhtarun Nessa and another vs. Habibullah & ors. reported in 31 D.L.R. (A D)88. Their Lordships of the Appellate Division have stated the law on the question as follows: 

 We have not been shown any other decision in which these views have been departed from. No specific objection, having been taken at any stage of the proceeding in the instant case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act before the learned Munsif as to non-joinder of any particular co-sharer or contiguous tenant, the opposite party shall be deemed to have waived the objection as to non-joinder. It is seen that P.W. 1 in his cross-examination disclosed the names of some contiguous tenants. Disclosure of the names of some persons who ought to have been impleaded in the proceeding would not make the application for pre-emption under section 96 of the Act bad on ground of defect of parties unless the pre-empee-opposite parties has raised the question of non- joinder of some co-sharer or contiguous tenant at the earliest opportunity before the learned Munsif. An issue for determination in a proceeding arises when a proposition of law and fact is asserted by one party and denied by other. The pre-emptee-opposite parties having not raised the issue as to non-joinder in their objection they cannot take advantage of any disclosure of such absence of any co-sharer at the trial and the learned Munsif as well is not required under law to decide the question of non-joinder. Since there was no contest between the parties as to the question of non-joinder in the pleading of the parties the application cannot fail for non-joinder of some contiguous tenants though disclosure about them were made during the cross-examination of the petitioner. 

 4. Mr. Md. Abdur Rahim, the learned Advocate for petitioner has next attacked the findings of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge that the application for pre-emption must fail because the learned Munsif made no finding on the question as to whether the pre-emptor-petitioners are persons to whom transfer by pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act could be made or in other words whether the pre-emptor petitioners were the person to whom transfer of the pre-empted land can be made under section 90 of the Act. The learned Subordinate Judge has also taken exception that no evidence was led by the pre-emptor- petitioners to prove that they were persons who are entitled to pre-empt the land in question under section 90 of the Act. The relevant portion of section 90 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act runs as follows; 

 "The statement to the effect that the petitioners are agriculturists and they owned 15/16 bighas of land and are entitled to pre-emption are false, fraudulent and collusive." 

 "3. It shall not be sufficient for a defendant in his written statement to deny generally the grounds alleged by the plaintiff but the defendant must deal specifically with each allegation of fact of which he does not admit the truth, except damages." 

 4. Every allegation of fact in the plaint, if not denied specifically or by necessary implication, or stated to be not admitted in the pleading of the defendant, shall be taken to be admitted except as against a person under disability. Provided that the court may in its discretion require any fact so admitted to be proved otherwise than by such admission." 

 10. The case of Nayeb Ali and others Vs. Aktar Rahman and others reported in 29 D.L.R. (High Court Division) 153 the learned Single Judge of this Court took a contrary view from that taken earlier in the case of Abdur Rahman Vs. Baser Ali and others. In the last cited case the pre-emptor asserted that section 90 of the Act was not an impediment in getting pre-emption. The pre-emptee did not deny the claim of the pre-emptor in his written objection. The learned Judge of this Division took the view that although there has been no denial of the statements as to the competency of the pre-emptor petitioner to get pre-emption still the pre-emptor was obliged to prove that the land if transferred to him by pre-emption will not exceed the statutory limit." The learned Single Judge held as follows: 

 11. The learned Judge departing from the decision reported in 21 D.L.R. (Dacca) page 599 took the view that the court while granting pre-emption was required under law to record a finding that the pre-emptor is a competent person under section 90 of the Act to get an order of pre-emption or that the pre-emptor was required to prove that if the land sought to be pre-empted was added the total quantity of land would not exceed the statutory limit of 100 standard bighas. We have also been referred to another decision of this court reported in 1 B.L.D. (High Court Division) 121 in the case of Anwara Begum Vs. Maimuna Khotun Chowdhury and others. In that decision A.T.M Afzal J. has agreed with the view expressed in the case reported in 21 D.L.R. (Dacca) and has differed from the view taken in 29 D.L.R. (High Court Division) 153 referred to above. A.T.M. Afzal, J. has held that if the statement as to competency of the petitioner had not been controverted by the pre-emptee opposite party the pre- emption cannot be denied on the ground that the court failed to record the necessary findings under section 90 of the Act. In the aforesaid case reported in 1 B.L.D. (H.C.D) 121 the learned Judge has also held that if the court failed to determine the issue the revisional court may determine the issue and record the necessary finding. The question is whether in the absence of any finding by the trial court as to whether pre-emptor is a person to whom transfer of the holding or a portion or share thereof as the case may be can be made under section 90, should the application for pre-emption fail. This question has been settled by a decision of Appellate Division of this Court in the case of Md. Matiur Rahman Vs. Md. Iman Ali @ Md. Iman Miah & others reported in 1 B.L.D (A.D) 280. In that decision their Lordships of the Appellate Division have held that in the absence of any finding by the trial Court as to whether the pre-emptor is a person to whom transfer by pre-emption can be made as envisaged under section 90 of the Act the application for pre-emption would not fail. Their Lordship have held that omission to record a finding to the effect that the pre-emptors were entitled to purchase or acquire the land by pre-emption and the total quantity of the land together with the land sought to be pre-empted would not execeed the maximum ceiling as set out in section 90 of the Act cannot be a ground for dismis3al of the pre-emption application. Their Lordships, however, remanded the case to the lower court for taking evidence on the point whether the petitioner was entitled to pre-empt the land under section 90 of the Act. This order of remand for taking evidence was made on the basis, it appears to us, on a prayer for remand by the pre-emptor stating that he would adduce evidence to support his case that he possessed only 10 bighas of land. This order of remand in the situation passed in that case in not applicable in the instant case before us. 

 12. In the instant case the pre-emptors averments regarding competency to get pre-emption as envisaged under section 90 have not been specifically denied. We are of opinion that under rule 1 of Order 14 and rules 3 and 5 of Order 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure absence of denial by the pre-emptee opposite party as to the assertion of the pre-emptor petition that they did not own more than 15/16 bighas of land the case does not call for any remand for the purpose of adducing any evidence on the point as envisaged under section 90 of the Act because the pre-emptee opposite parties have not pleaded that the total land added up to the land sought to be pre-empted would exceed the ceiling as set out under section 90 of the Act The pleadings of the pre-emptor as envisaged under section 90 of the Act as to ceiling of land having not been specifically denied or set up-as a defence the pre-emptee opposite party would be precluded under law to adduce evidence to controvert the assertion made by the pre-emptor This view has also been taken, by Mustafa Kamal J. in his reference to the learned Chief Justice for a decision by a Divisional Bench. In the facts and circumstances of the case an order or remand to enable the pre-emptors to adduce evidence in support of their assertion of fact as envisaged under the provision under section 90 of the Act would be a fruitless endeavor and without any purpose. The parties on the point in question being not in variance there is no point for remand for decision by-the trial Court. Under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure this Court is competent to make a finding on the basis of materials available in the record The assertions that the pre-emptor petitioners would not own a total of more than 100 standard bighas together with the land sought to be pre-empted having not been denied and specifically set up in defence the statement in the application for pre-emption may be taken to have been admitted by the pre-emptee petitioners as being competent persons to whom transfer of the land or a portion or share thereof can be made under section 90 of the Act. In this view the application for pre- emption must succeed.
